documents.abstract: Legends and fairytales often centre on caution: Māui used a careful plan to slow the Sun, while Little Red Riding Hood sensed something was wrong with her grandmother. Kia Tūpato is a traditional Māori expression meaning caution. Rooted in Polynesian culture, it has moved through two key phases: its adoption by Māori and its continued use after European settlement. It is now entering a third phase as a digital workplace tool. This oral presentation traces the history of Kia Tūpato, presents findings from two recent case studies, and explores its use in workplaces and its emerging role as a digital app. The case studies show how Kia Tūpato can help workers make safer decisions, connect more effectively with workplace systems, and engage with decision-makers. Grounded in culture and practical relevance for Māori and many blue-collar workers, Kia Tūpato gives human factors and ergonomics practitioners a clear example of how cultural predispositions can shape worker decisions and support safer behaviour.

This study examines the most critical aeronautical occurrence scenarios involving helicopters in Brazil from 2016 to 2025, aiming to establish an exploratory framework to guide flight-safety mitigation strategies. Grounded in a quantitative approach utilizing official CENIPA data, the investigation incorporated Pareto diagrams and the Consequence and Recurrence Matrix (MCR). The findings identify Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) and Low Altitude Operation (LALT) as the most critical event types. Mechanical-failure categories (SCF-PP, SCF-NP) also demonstrated significant prevalence, suggesting a potential relationship with maintenance-related operational factors. In conclusion, addressing these operational risks demands a sociotechnical framework through robust Safety Management Systems (SMS) and the enhancement of CRM and MRM training protocols across both cockpit and hangar environments.

HeritageLens is an AI-powered Augmented Reality (AR) heritage guide designed to make exploring historical monuments more interactive and informative. Traditional methods of heritage exploration, such as information boards, printed materials and guided tours, often provide limited interaction and may not fully explain the historical importance of monuments. This paper presents HeritageLens, a system that combines Computer Vision-based monument recognition, historical information, AI-powered conversational assistance and location-based heritage discovery. It also explores features such as audio storytelling, multilingual explanations and AR-based visualisation to improve the overall learning experience. The application is designed to help tourists, students and heritage enthusiasts discover monuments, understand their historical significance and access information through a single platform. The paper discusses the system architecture, related research, development methodology, technologies used, evaluation framework and possible future improvements. The proposed system aims to make cultural heritage more accessible through the integration of Artificial Intelligence, Computer Vision and Augmented Reality technologies.

Large language models (LLMs) can provide voters information about political issues, party positions, and even advise on which party to vote for. However, no previous study explores whether off-the-shelf LLMs could be used as voting advice applications (VAAs) to improve voter-party congruence. In this article, we address this gap by examining how Gemini 3 Flash advises a sample of 6,022 German survey respondents on which party to vote for, based on their policy preferences and priorities alone. In brief, we find that for most respondents, following the LLM’s advice would benefit voter-party policy alignment (i.e. congruence), with a significantly stronger remedial effect among voters with low levels of political interest and formal education. However, our analysis also reveals concerning biases in the LLM’s recommendations. For instance, the LLM suggested voting for the AfD at ~1.5 times the frequency of a standard salience-weighted proximity model. In addition, the LLM hardly ever advised voting for either Die Linke or the BSW. We conclude that while LLMs can approximate the behaviour of VAAs, users should be aware that the LLM’s recommendations are still biased in ways that are extremely difficult to trace.

Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) can transform teaching, learning, assessment and research in higher education. In Ecuador, the adoption of ChatGPT, Gemini and other language models is driving academic interest, yet little is known about the scientific production that addresses it. This systematic mapping review, reported in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020 statement, maps the scientific production on generative artificial intelligence that explicitly refers to Ecuador, indexed in Scopus and the Web of Science Core Collection between 2024 and 2026, in order to establish the weight that higher education holds within it. No disciplinary filter was applied to the query, so that this weight could be measured rather than assumed. The search, executed on 4 July 2026, retrieved 57 records (all 16 Web of Science records were also in Scopus, so the corpus comes in practice from Scopus; regional databases were not searched); after removing 16 duplicates and excluding 9 records, 32 documents were mapped with bibliometric indicators (Bibliometrix, VOSviewer), and the 18 higher education studies with primary data were subjected to a focused synthesis that included the appraisal of their methodological quality with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool. Higher education accounts for 20 of the 32 documents (63%); the other 12 are spread over political communication and journalism, legal and technical applications and four smaller domains. A sensitivity search with synonyms, Spanish terms and the year 2023, run on 15 October 2026, gave a similar share (44 of 73 documents, 60%). Within the higher education corpus, perceptions and acceptance of GAI are the most frequent outcome domain (16 of 18 studies); learning outcomes appear in six, but only two measure them directly. Eight studies use descriptive or cross-sectional designs, and none is randomised or longitudinal. ChatGPT is the most frequently examined tool (11 of 18). Sample representativeness and control of confounding were the most frequent methodological weaknesses. The findings highlight the need for experimental and longitudinal research evaluating the impact of GAI on Ecuadorian higher education.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) offer a potential approach to inferring standardized questionnaire responses from qualitative interviews, but their utility for assessing parenting remains unclear. We evaluated six generative LLMs using zero-shot prompting to infer responses to the Multidimensional Assessment of Parenting Scale (MAPS) from interviews with 43 parents. Models inferred responses to 35 MAPS items from two introductory questions about family, parenting roles, and the meaning of caregiving. Performance was evaluated through exact item-response agreement, correlations between inferred and self-reported parenting scores, systematic score differences, and internal consistency. Across models, Fisher-averaged correlations between inferred and self-reported MAPS subscale scores ranged from .320 to .434, with no consistently superior model. Correlations were strongest and most consistent for Warmth, whereas Physical Control showed little correspondence and substantial floor restriction. Across parent–item pairs, 35.5%–44.7% of inferred responses exactly matched parents’ selected response categories. All models assigned systematically lower response categories than parents and rarely selected the highest category; score underestimation was particularly evident for Positive Parenting. Model-derived subscales generally showed internal consistency, although higher internal consistency did not consistently correspond to stronger correlations with parent-reported scores. Exploratory analyses indicated modest similarity in the associations of inferred and self-reported parenting scores with other psychological constructs. Preliminary comparisons also suggested that shorter interview segments substantially reduced computational requirements without clear evidence of poorer performance. These findings support further evaluation of LLM-based parenting assessment while highlighting limitations in reproducing individual responses, matching score levels, and capturing some parenting dimensions.

documents.abstract: The rapidly expanding generative AI landscape brings together methods that differ in architecture, learning objective, mathematical representation and sampling procedure. A concise, selectively organised technical guide can provide an accessible starting point for developing a coherent understanding of this increasingly complex landscape. This article takes a generation-centred approach, connecting how models produce new observations with the modelling and learning principles that make generation possible. We develop a two-level perspective: first, distinguishing three recurring generation routes-direct transformation or decoding, sequential conditional construction, and iterative updating or transport; and second, examining the modelling and learning principles underlying these routes. Representative approaches are introduced through their key components, learning objectives and sampling procedures. We then examine their broader connections, including how different architectures and generation mechanisms can overlap or be combined. By bringing together essential technical explanations within a compact conceptual framework, the article aims to help readers develop a working understanding of unfamiliar approaches, recognise connections among models they have encountered, and navigate different approaches within the broader generative AI landscape.

documents.abstract: Rubric-based reinforcement learning constructs rewards for aligning large language models with human preferences, typically by equally aggregating continuous scores that a judge assigns to individual criteria. However, scoring heterogeneity across criteria can distort candidate rankings. Existing work has focused on improving judges, learning criterion weights, or refining aggregation, whereas the interaction between scoring heterogeneity and ranking remains insufficiently understood. We formalize this heterogeneity as \emph{reward gain imbalance}: each criterion enters the aggregated reward with its own reward gain, the gap between its expected scores on satisfied and unsatisfied responses. Counterintuitively, our experiments show that removing this imbalance, even with ground-truth labels, lowers ranking accuracy. To explain this, we derive an exact decomposition of the reward difference between any two candidates into a base satisfaction signal, a reward gain imbalance term, and a residual term, showing that reward gain imbalance can attenuate or amplify the base signal, and finding that misrankings usually concentrate on pairs where it attenuates. Guided by this analysis, we propose the adaptive \textbf{D}ual-\textbf{C}enter \textbf{C}lipping aggregation (DCC), which bounds each criterion's contribution to the reward difference instead of simply removing the imbalance. Using only the scores of the current candidate group, it determines a clipping interval that imposes a common upper bound on per-criterion score differences between candidates, limiting the excessive influence of extreme scores while preserving continuous judgment information....

documents.abstract: To achieve his ideal of the Great Harmony (Datong), Confucius envisioned a society founded on the altruistic principle that “The world belongs to all”. Yet, inherent human self-interest has long rendered this vision utopian. The rise of the decentralized market economy in modern times has reframed the objective of resource allocation toward guiding self-interested individuals to achieve Pareto optimality—a state that resonates deeply with Confucius’ injunction: “Do not impose on others what you yourself do not desire.” Although the conditions for a fully functional decentralized market are highly demanding, advances in information technology and artificial intelligence are increasingly enabling us to approach them, thereby revitalizing the feasibility of a Datong society. However, a critical caveat remains: if general artificial intelligence evolves to serve only a minority rather than all equally, society could be driven in a direction diametrically opposed to the ideal of Great Harmony.

Introduction This study explores media narratives of violence in Mexico through a hybrid human-computer interaction workflow combining computational analysis, human interpretation and generative artificial intelligence. Methods A non-probability corpus of 105 news items was analyzed to identify recurring terms, actors, locations and semantic relationships. Corpus summaries informed a workshop with 15 participants, who developed definitions and recursively refined text prompts and AI-generated images across five iterations. Textual and visual changes were analyzed, and experts supported their synthesis into an infographic and video. Results The selected corpus and workshop materials showed variation in textual and visual representations. Computational summaries made selected semantic differences explicit, while participants and experts supplied contextual interpretation. The process produced an infographic and video integrating these materials. Discussion The exploratory design does not estimate population parameters or establish causal effects. The workflow illustrates a human-led collaborative approach informed by mixed-initiative design: computational methods support structured comparison and generative variation, while people provide interpretation and critical judgment.

Available-to-promise (ATP) systems increasingly rely on machine learning to predict delivery dates under conditions of fluctuating supply, capacity constraints, and demand variability. Yet purely algorithmic ATP pipelines face a persistent adoption barrier: planners and account teams frequently override or distrust automated delivery-date predictions, particularly after observing even isolated forecasting errors, a pattern long documented in the algorithm-aversion literature. Conversely, human-only override regimes reintroduce the inconsistency and latency that automation was meant to eliminate. This paper proposes a human-in-the-loop (HITL) available-to-promise intelligence framework that resolves this tension by design rather than by policy. Following a design science research approach, the framework separates delivery-date prediction into four architectural layers: an algorithmic prediction layer, a confidence and uncertainty estimation layer, a human-review trigger layer governed by explicit escalation criteria, and an override/feedback-capture layer that closes the loop back into model governance. The trigger layer operationalises when a prediction should reach a human reviewer, using confidence thresholds, anomalous order-pattern detection, and value/risk tiering rather than blanket human review or blanket automation. The paper situates this design against literature on algorithm aversion and appreciation, human-in-the-loop machine learning architectures, and explainability in supply-chain artificial intelligence and evaluates the framework's utility against design science research criteria rather than primary empirical validation. The paper closes with an explicit limitations discussion and a concrete agenda for the multi-case empirical validation the framework's real-world deployment would require.

documents.abstract: Recent research on the use of Large Language Models (LLMs) reports divergent cognitive outcomes, including improved assisted performance, limited transfer, and compromised unaided learning. Here, we argue that part of this seeming inconsistency arises because studies often assess different cognitive systems without making the unit of analysis explicit. Building on work in extended and distributed cognition, we propose the Human-LLM Cognitive Extension (HLCE) as a methodological framework for matching experimental designs, measures, and causal inferences to four distinct systems: the human acting independently, the artificial agent, the joined human-LLM configuration, and the human after division. The framework also treats the coupling architecture as part of the experimental object. HLCE separates performance augmentation, system-level complementarity, post-interaction human change, and stronger claims of constitutive cognitive integration. This separation can improve the interpretation of existing evidence and guide the design of human-LLM interactions without assuming in advance that these configurations constitute extended minds. We illustrate the application of HLCE with a synthetic diagnostic experiment comparing two connecting configurations that differ in how supporting information is communicated. The example highlights how distinct couplings can shape the organization of joint problem-solving, even when the final outcome remains unchanged. Overall, HLCE provides a methodological basis for designing controlled experiments and interpreting evidence across distinct forms of human-LLM cognitive interaction.

Human–AI Charter Public Consultation: 14 Key Questions on Governability, Risk Control and Room to Develop This discussion paper invites public comment on the Human–AI Charter (Public Consultation Draft). Its central idea is to govern how AI capabilities are translated into real-world power, not intelligence itself. AI may learn, reason and research freely; but when it gains the ability to move money, operate equipment, touch infrastructure or decide on someone's behalf, that power must have a lawful source and clear limits, and stay provable, reviewable and open to remedy. The paper sets out 14 open questions in four groups: governability (G1–G4), risk control (R1–R4), room to develop (D1–D3), and legitimacy and the future (L1–L3). It also includes two candidate new clauses for consultation, not yet part of the charter text: (A) responsibility registers for high-risk AI, and (B) an independent public forum for users as a "fourth estate" of AI governance. This consultation remains open, with no closing date. Please send comments, quoting the question number (e.g. G2, R3), to humanaicharter@gmail.com. documents.abstract: Natural language explanations produced by large language models (LLMs) are often persuasive, but not necessarily scrutable: users cannot easily verify whether the claims in an explanation are supported by evidence. In XAI, this motivates a focus on faithfulness and traceability, i.e., the extent to which an explanation’s claims can be grounded in, and traced back to, an explicit source. We study these desiderata in retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) for programming education, where textbooks provide authoritative evidence. We benchmark six LLMs on 90 Stack Overflow questions grounded in three programming textbooks and quantify source faithfulness via source adherence metrics. We find that non Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models have median source adherence of 0%, while baseline RAG systems still exhibit low median adherence (22–40%, depending on the model). Motivated by Achinstein’s illocutionary theory of explanation, we introduce illocutionary macro-planning as a descriptive design principle for source-faithful explanations and instantiate it with chain-of-illocution prompting (CoI), which expands a query into implicit explanatory questions that drive retrieval. Across models, CoI yields statistically significant gains (up to 63%) in source adherence, although absolute adherence remains moderate and the gains are weak or non-significant for some models. A user study with 165 retained participants (220 recruited) indicates that these gains do not harm satisfaction, relevance, or perceived correctness. Data and Code: https://github.com/Francesco-Sovrano/chain-of-illocution

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) to support assessment and feedback in higher education has attracted growing interest, but concerns remain about the consistency and appropriateness of AI-generated grades in summative contexts. This study examined whether a combined calibration strategy involving a more explicit rubric and marking prompt could improve agreement between AI-assisted grading and educator judgement in a laboratory-based STEM assessment. We compared educator-assigned marks for 40 graduate Electrochemical Energy Storage Systems laboratory reports with marks generated by GPT-5 under pre- and post-calibration configurations, and examined agreement using complementary statistical and visual analyses. Following calibration, agreement with educator marks improved across measures of score correspondence and absolute agreement: the intraclass correlation coefficient increased from 0.818 to 0.928, the mean AI-educator difference decreased from +1.625 to +1.041 marks, and no post-calibration report differed from the educator mark by more than 10 marks. These findings suggest that the way assessment criteria, evidence requirements, and marking rules are specified can materially influence AI-human grading agreement. However, the revised rubric and prompt were introduced together, calibration drew on discrepancies observed in the same 40 reports used for post-calibration evaluation, and one educator's marks served as the reference. The results therefore support improved in-sample agreement under a human-supervised calibration strategy, rather than establishing grading validity or interchangeability for autonomous summative decisions.

Clinical studies regularly ask participants to describe their experiences in their own words. These open-ended questions are included so that participants can report what they themselves consider relevant, and ideally researchers want to harvest this information. In practice however, these responses are rarely analyzed and often effectively discarded, since translating them into a useful quantitative format for further analysis traditionally required trained coders or advanced technical skills. Current transformer-based language models offer an appealing alternative option to quantify text: they internally represent any text input as high-dimensional numerical representations called text embeddings. Fromavailable open-weight models, these text embeddings can be freely extracted on a local machine. As text embeddings are just vectors of numbers, they can be plugged as predictors into standard statistical analyses. Here, we applied this to three large datasets in which participants described their experiences in the context of psychedelic substance use. We investigated whether text embeddings of these free-text descriptions improve cross-validated, held-out predictions of clinically relevant outcomes (well-being, change in well-being, change in psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity, post-traumatic growth) after we control for a range of other predictors capturingdemographic information, the setting of the experience, and a series of questionnaire data. We found reliable increases in predictive accuracy for three of the five outcomes (change in well-being and psychological flexibility, post-traumatic symptom severity), in two of the three datasets. Some of these increases are substantial. We therefore recommend (where possible) the inclusion of open-ended questions in any questionnaire, and to actually pass this information to analysis, to efficiently capture valuable information that would otherwise be lost.

Speciation maintains distinct subpopulations in evolutionary search through similarity-based grouping and species-aware parent selection. For text-based individuals, niches depend on both the compatibility representation and the assignment operator that turns pairwise relations into species. We examine this design space in black-box evolutionary red teaming of large language models, comparing embedding and natural language inference (NLI) dissimilarities under representative-based and density-based speciation. Offline calibration on a 3,139-prompt archive shows that MiniLM embedding dissimilarity ($d_E$) and DeBERTa-v3-small NLI non-entailment ($d_{\neg E}$) produce different species structures at the same nominal threshold. Even with pairwise edge density matched to MiniLM, NLI density connectivity forms a few concentrated, mixed-topic species, with substantially more off-topic membership. These structural differences persist online under a matched evaluation budget. The endpoint top-50 median fitness favors incremental DBSCAN over leader-follower, but bootstrap intervals from 10 runs include zero, providing no reliable evidence of an advantage. Semantic diversity among top prompts declines in every configuration, with no consistent method advantage. The clearest difference concerns high-fitness population occupancy: MiniLM incremental DBSCAN maintains mature niches across seed topics, whereas NLI incremental DBSCAN attains the same highest observed median fitness while concentrating high-fitness prompts in variants of a few seed topics. Thus, representation-dependent connectivity predicts population structure more consistently than endpoint fitness. Species count alone does not establish quality-diversity, and more species do not necessarily preserve semantically diverse high-fitness prompts.

DESCRIPTION This collection brings together fifteen independently authored research essays and analytical works examining artificial intelligence, social structures, political authority, economic inequality, cybersecurity, digital identity, institutional accountability, and the changing relationship between individuals and complex technological systems. Originally published as individual works through Substack, these essays approach contemporary technological and social transformations from multiple disciplinary perspectives. Some investigate technical and epistemic limitations in AI systems, cybersecurity, information infrastructure, and digital continuity. Others examine political polarization, religious authority, generational inheritance, labor-market exclusion, economic stratification, institutional recognition, and the distribution of power. Several works also explore questions concerning the reconstruction of personal identity through informational systems, the relationship between memory and continuity, and the consequences of transferring human judgment or authority into increasingly autonomous technological environments. The collection does not advance a single unified theory or claim that all included works share the same methodology. Instead, it documents an evolving independent research program organized around several recurring questions: What happens when the systems used to observe reality become incapable of representing the conditions that actually exist? How do institutions, political structures, and economic arrangements determine who receives opportunities, recognition, and the benefits of collective contribution? How are memory, identity, authority, and inherited social structures transformed when technological systems begin to mediate increasingly fundamental aspects of human life? Why do institutions repeatedly struggle to address structural vulnerabilities even when their underlying causes are already identifiable? And what forms of accountability, institutional adaptation, and technical architecture are necessary when existing systems can no longer reliably manage the complexity they have created? The works included here range from technical proposals and systems analysis to political and socioeconomic commentary, conceptual frameworks, and exploratory scenarios. Their evidentiary foundations and analytical methods therefore vary according to their respective subjects. Together, they examine a recurring structural problem: the growing distance between what complex systems represent, what institutions reward, what individuals experience, and what society is actually capable of verifying. This collection should be understood as an archival record of independent research and analysis rather than a unified theoretical framework. documents.abstract: AI agents driven by foundation models have shown potential for industrial automation beyond rule-based control. However, existing studies differ in how industrial agents collaborate and how their systems are tested, making it difficult to compare networking requirements and physical execution capabilities. This paper examines the intersection of networked agents and industrial automation, where industrial signals, communication constraints, contextual information, and operational requirements must be considered jointly. It develops the Industrial Internet of Agents (IIoA) and presents a conceptual architecture for analyzing industrial deployment requirements. Building on the Internet of Agents (IoA) framework, IIoA re-specifies sensing, communication, decision-making, and execution through eleven industrial extensions. Representative studies are synthesized across shopfloor operations, autonomous plant operations and maintenance, supply chain collaboration, and digital twin systems. The analysis indicates that industrial agent networking requires the joint design of semantic coordination, operational technology (OT) interoperability, latency-aware deployment, trust governance, and verifiable physical execution. Finally, seven open challenges are identified, covering reliability, latency, protocol integrity, scalability, physical grounding, adaptability, and evaluation.

This conceptual paper introduces Inferential Disclosure Through Joined Fragments, a mechanism by which separately disclosed pieces of information become available to one reader, who can connect them to infer a relationship that no piece established alone. The paper asks how strongly the evidence supports the connection and whether the purposes for which the fragments were disclosed permit their combined use. A reader may have strong grounds for an identification while permission to make that use of the records remains unsettled. The first case concerns the Japanese designator “AF” before the Battle of Midway. By March 1942, analysts at Corregidor had identified AF as Midway, while disagreement persisted in Washington. In May, Midway sent an uncoded message reporting a shortage of fresh water. A subsequent Japanese report attributed a water shortage to AF. The shared detail connected the two messages and corroborated the earlier identification. The second case concerns AOL’s 2006 release of search queries grouped under user numbers. One number brought together searches mentioning a town, a surname, and a housing subdivision. Reporters followed those clues to Thelma Arnold, who recognized the searches as her own. She explained that she had researched some symptoms for friends. The evidence supported identifying who had conducted the searches while leaving open whom any particular search described. The paper places this case alongside Latanya Sweeney’s work on re-identification through linked records. Part of the Sources and Evidentiary Limits series within On Human Modeling, the paper also offers a distinction relevant to human–AI interaction. A draft exhibition program might list a title and booking code, while a venue’s schedule lists the same code and a room. An AI assistant could infer where the exhibition is planned. Whether the organizers authorized combining those records for a public announcement is a separate question.

documents.abstract: This conceptual paper introduces Inquiry-Induced Depletion of Later Examination Capacity, an account of how one inquiry can consume a resource that a later inquiry also needs. The resource may be material, time, attention, or cooperation. A check can answer its immediate question accurately and still leave a later question harder to examine. The cost depends on what that later question requires and how much of the resource remains available to answer it. The paper sets out three requirements for identifying depletion. An assessment must name the shared resource, establish what the earlier inquiry consumed, and identify a later question whose examination depended on what was lost. This requires comparing what was available before and after the inquiry and considering other causes of the loss. A record may preserve enough evidence for a particular later question, attention may recover, and learning from the first inquiry may offset some of its cost. The paper places the mechanism alongside the 1992 Valletta Convention’s provision for archaeological reserves and examines two documented cases. Near Xi’an, excavation exposed the painted terracotta figures of the First Emperor of Qin. Once exposed, the lacquer beneath the pigment could flake away within minutes, taking with it evidence of the figures’ original colors. Apollo 17 sample 73001 illustrates preservation. NASA kept the lunar sample sealed for nearly 50 years. In 2022, researchers used X-ray computed tomography to record the core’s internal arrangement before removing and dividing it for study. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can sequence or stop an examination and who bears the cost when a shared resource runs low. A potential application in human–AI evaluation is the allocation of reviewer time. If an AI assistant requests several routine checks before a deadline, an evaluator could trace how much time those checks consumed and whether the reviewer still had enough time to examine a disputed source on which the final judgment depended.

Modern sociotechnical systems—spanning sovereign signals intelligence, hyperscale semiconductor supply chains, connected automotive infrastructure, and frontier artificial intelligence laboratories—exhibit a recurring divergence between physical system state (C) and institutional representation (I). When architectural shortcuts, default-open perimeters, or circular capital commitments generate structural failures, governing bodies rarely initiate immediate remediation. Instead, they execute a standardized crisis-containment protocol termed The Ba Sing Se Doctrine: an active administrative posture that suppresses internal error signals until an external leak forces public visibility, at which point the institution issues formal decrees reclassifying systemic breaches as routine maintenance, isolated personal errors, or resolved minor friction. Tracing this mechanism from classical imperial theater at the Hellespont and the English Channel to four concurrent November 2026 infrastructure and technology crises, this paper formalizes the structural anatomy of zero-admission governance and demonstrates why narrative equilibrium accelerates physical collapse.

Safety culture, psychosocial safety, work design and worker well-being are increasingly considered together, although they describe different organisational conditions, processes and outcomes. We conducted a safety-culture-anchored conceptual review informed by structured bibliographic searching and purposive source selection to examine these boundaries. Searches of Scopus and Web of Science on 29 June 2026 identified 3129 records. A dated duplicate audit reconciled 2500 report records; 28 verified complete texts from a 44-source conceptual set supported detailed synthesis. Recurrent organisational practices concerned management commitment, enacted priorities, resources, communication, participation, justice and feedback for improvement. Their recurrence did not establish a single higher-order construct. The synthesis compares referents, levels, mechanisms, measurement and outcomes across safety, psychosocial-health and well-being approaches. It provides explicit rules for connecting these entities without treating their measures or outcomes as interchangeable. Three conditional propositions specify future tests of construct discrimination, cross-domain pathways and diagnostic usefulness. Purposive selection, incomplete records of later selection decisions, unequal coverage of adjacent fields and the absence of documented independent duplicate screening limit coverage and reproducibility. The proposed framework is a conceptual interpretation, not a validated causal model.

This study aims to analyze the extent to which current Brazilian labor legislation is sufficient to protect workers subject to algorithmic management through artificial intelligence systems. It seeks to understand the impact of these technologies on labor relations, particularly regarding legal subordination, control mechanisms, and the risks arising from their use. To this end, qualitative bibliographic and documentary research was conducted through the analysis of legislation, legal scholarship, scientific articles, institutional documents, and case law related to artificial intelligence and worker protection. The results demonstrate that Brazilian legislation provides legal instruments capable of protecting workers against algorithmic management, particularly Articles 2, 3, and 6, sole paragraph, of the Consolidation of Labor Laws (CLT), as well as provisions concerning non-pecuniary damages and civil liability. The study also found that algorithmic subordination may constitute legal subordination, since computerized systems can perform command, control, and supervision functions. However, challenges were identified regarding the effectiveness of legal protection, judicial interpretation, and liability for damages arising from these technologies. It is concluded that the Brazilian legal system provides an adaptable normative framework for worker protection, but its effectiveness depends on the proper application of existing legal provisions, the development of case law, and the ability to address the challenges posed by technological advancement.

Introduction. Artificial intelligence has expanded opportunities for personalized learning in basic education through tools capable of adapting content, providing feedback, and addressing diverse educational needs. The objective of this study was to analyze artificial intelligence applications in personalized learning, identifying pedagogical opportunities, implementation challenges, and research trends. Methodology. A scoping review was developed following the methodological guidance of the Joanna Briggs Institute and the PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. The bibliographic selection exercise covered publications from 2020 to 2026, considering Scopus, Web of Science, ERIC, and SciELO. Results. The methodological flow included 420 identified records, 90 duplicates removed, and 330 records screened. Following the screening and eligibility stages, a set of 25 studies was established for thematic synthesis. The results were organized into five categories: adaptive systems and intelligent tutoring, generative artificial intelligence, AI literacy and teacher mediation, equity and ethics, and implementation and evaluation. The literature examined revealed opportunities related to content adaptation, individualized support, immediate feedback, and academic progress monitoring. Challenges associated with data protection, algorithmic bias, digital inequalities, and teacher preparation were also identified. Conclusions. It is concluded that artificial intelligence offers relevant possibilities for diversifying learning experiences, although its educational integration requires pedagogical supervision, ethical criteria, and contextualized evaluations to establish its actual contributions.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Disease-outbreak information is spread across surveillance reports, environmental observations and population statistics,and public-health users need it presented in a form they can inspectand question. This paper presents the design and implementationof an SDG 3 health platform that combines a multi-factor outbreak risk-scoring module, a what-if climate-variation analysis, acollaborative multi-agent chatbot, a locally hosted Mistral 7B Instruct model accessed through LM Studio, a retrieval-groundedknowledge module, and a heuristic hallucination detector for usersubmitted outbreak reports. The risk module combines new cases,rainfall, humidity, temperature, population density and hospitaladmissions into a weighted score from 0 to 100, classifies it as Low,Medium or High, and derives four-week and three-month projections. A React front end communicates with a FastAPI back endthat provides JWT authentication, role-based access, an administrator review workflow with audit events, and report generation. Thelanguage model communicates information only; it does not compute risk scores. The platform does not forecast case counts witha time-series model. A Random Forest classifier for risk-categoryclassification (Low, Medium, High) was evaluated on a balancedtest set of 90 samples and reached 88.89% accuracy and a macroF1-score of 88.89%. The worked examples of the scoring rules arenot accuracy measurements, and learned time-series forecasting,such as LSTM, is identified as future work.Keywords—Disease outbreak risk assessment, generative AI, multiagent systems, Mistral, LM Studio, retrieval-augmented generation,hallucination detection, public health, SDG 3.

documents.abstract: Intent contracts are an authorization interface for tool-using LLM agents in which the planning model holds no tools. For each step it submits a short logged contract: a goal, a verbatim quotation of the user, and scope fields. Code validates the contract, and a small trusted model checks it against the user's words and writes the tool call itself. Provided the validation and dispatch code is correct, every executed call is written by the trusted model, the planner's influence on a call is confined to a contract logged before it, and the trusted side decides how much of a request to carry out. We compare contracts with two reviewers of planner-written commands: one sees only the user's words and the command, the information boundary of a reasoning-blind permission classifier, and one also sees the planner's goal and a checked quotation. With gpt-6.1-terra as planner and GLM-5.3-Flash as the trusted model on three AmPermBench task families, every object changed under contracts is named in the goal of the contract that produced the change; under review the planner names objects in its commands and rarely in its goals. When the planner adds work the user never asked for, contracts complete the user's task in 27/30 runs and the intent-visible reviewer in 16/30, because a reviewer can only refuse a whole command. Contracts do not reduce unauthorized actions. They are indistinguishable from blind review, and once the benchmark's environment terms are clarified, every condition that changes state hits a wrong target in 40-49% of those runs. That error is the planner's choice of objects for an ambiguous reference, which no trusted model here can see the environment to check; telling the executor to decline when unsure does not change it. We evaluate benign over-reach with one pair of models, not adversarial planners. We release the plugin and run records.

documents.abstract: Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GAI) has emerged as a new source of academic support for university students. However, students' willingness to seek academic help may also be influenced by social evaluation concerns surrounding traditional interpersonal help-seeking. This study examines how academic help-seeking (AHS) stigma relates to interpersonal help-seeking avoidance through academic shame, and whether interpersonal avoidance is associated with GAI help-seeking tendency under different levels of perceived anonymity. Methods Two independent cross-sectional survey studies were conducted among Chinese university students. Study 1 examined the relationships among AHS stigma, academic shame, and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance using data from 183 undergraduate students. Study 2 extended the model with a sample of 401 university students by examining the relationship between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency, as well as the moderating role of perceived anonymity. PLS-SEM was used to test the proposed relationships. Results Across both studies, AHS stigma was positively associated with interpersonal help-seeking avoidance. Academic shame showed significant indirect associations between AHS stigma and interpersonal help-seeking avoidance in both studies. Study 2 further showed that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance was positively associated with GAI help-seeking tendency. Moreover, perceived anonymity positively moderated this relationship, such that the positive association between interpersonal help-seeking avoidance and GAI help-seeking tendency was stronger at higher levels of perceived anonymity. Discussion The findings highlight the social-emotional dimensions of academic help-seeking, showing that interpersonal help-seeking avoidance can coexist with a greater willingness to seek support from GAI tools. Perceived anonymity further conditions this association, suggesting that the perceived social visibility of help-seeking is relevant to students' support preferences. These findings extend the understanding of GAI-assisted academic help-seeking beyond technology-related considerations, while distinguishing help-seeking tendencies from actual changes in support-source use.

The expression of emotions in sculptures is conveyed through structural forms, spatial relationships, material characteristics, and symbolic elements. However, traditional artistic analysis mainly relies on expert interpretation, making emotional expression difficult to quantify. With the development of computer vision and multimodal Artificial Intelligence (AI), deep learning approaches provide new opportunities for visual art understanding. Nevertheless, existing methods still face challenges in establishing connections between visual features and abstract emotional semantics, as well as providing interpretable prediction processes. To address these issues, an interpretive model of emotional expression in sculptures based on visual-affective semantic analysis is proposed. A public sculpture image dataset containing 1,800 instances is constructed. A 50-layer Residual Network (ResNet50) is employed to extract morphological and textural features, while Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training (CLIP) is used to establish associations between visual representations and affective semantics. An attention-based fusion mechanism integrates visual and semantic features for emotion classification. Gradient-weighted Class Activation Mapping (Grad-CAM) and semantic ablation methods are further applied to analyze the decision-making process of the model. Experimental results show that the visual-semantic fusion model achieves an accuracy of 82.59% and a Macro-averaged F1 score (Macro-F1) of 80.73% on the test set, outperforming the ResNet50 visual model with 76.30% accuracy and 75.67% Macro-F1, as well as the CLIP semantic model with 73.85% accuracy and 72.58% Macro-F1. Interpretation analysis demonstrates that the model mainly focuses on essential artistic elements, including posture, contour, and spatial structure, with strong consistency with expert evaluations. This research provides an effective artificial intelligence framework for sculptural emotion analysis and offers potential applications in digital museums, art education, intelligent retrieval systems, and computational cultural heritage studies.

This conceptual paper introduces Irreducible-Realization Classification Protecting a Settled Model, a mechanism through which calling a surprising result ordinary variation can keep a model or one of its assumptions from being reopened. The mechanism applies when the classification itself prevents diagnostic inquiry and the model’s account of uncertainty gives inadequate grounds for that decision. The paper asks what the model projected, what range or probability distribution supported that projection, and how the observed departure compared with it. A well-supported account of uncertainty can justify leaving a model in place after a surprising result. Possibility alone gives little guidance about whether a departure of this size warrants investigation. Identifying the mechanism also requires evidence that the classification actually stopped inquiry. A public description of a result as bad luck can coexist with an investigation already underway. The paper places the mechanism alongside Nassim Nicholas Taleb’s account of highly improbable events and examines two documented cases. Casino consultant Eliot Jacobson recalled initially attributing a report about the Lucky Lucky blackjack side bet to ordinary variation. Further reports prompted an analysis showing that players could gain an advantage by choosing when to bet. The published accounts provide no casino results from which to estimate the probability of the initial report. The 2011 OPERA neutrino measurement illustrates a different response. The apparent early arrival was large relative to the stated timing uncertainties, and the collaboration invited scrutiny. Subsequent investigation traced the anomaly to a fault in the fiber-optic timing system. Part of the Recursive Inquiry and Encounter series within On Human Modeling, the paper asks who can inspect the uncertainty estimate behind a decision to close an inquiry. A potential application in human–AI evaluation is a transit planner’s review of an unexpectedly long wait. If the planner closes the review because an AI forecast allows occasional delays, an evaluator could ask how often the forecast predicted waits that long under comparable conditions and what evidence supported that estimate.

documents.abstract: Backgrounds: Islamic financial planning can connect household resilience, ethical investment and social redistribution within a coherent life-cycle framework. Objectives: This article updates the supplied manuscript by integrating comparative documentary evidence from Saudi Arabia, Malaysia, Indonesia, Türkiye and Pakistan with a proposed digitally enabled operational model. Methodology: A structured narrative review distinguishes observed institutional developments from normative design choices and untested impact propositions. Findings: The model retains four interdependent pillars: wealth protection, accumulation, preservation and distribution. It adds explicit cash flow management, affordable access, consumer protection and measurable wellbeing outcomes. Contemporary official evidence demonstrates the scale of Islamic finance and the feasibility of retail sukuk, social takaful, value-based intermediation and cash waqf-linked sukuk, but does not establish that a comprehensive planning service has caused improvements in household welfare. Blockchain, artificial intelligence, machine learning, the Internet of Things and big data can support traceability, forecasting and monitoring when governed by consent, legal enforceability, Shariah review and human accountability. The article proposes a mind map, implementation sequence and evaluation design. Conclusions: Universal access is a central service principle; religion-specific obligations and legally restricted funds require separate treatment. The resulting framework offers testable pathways toward financial resilience and sustainable development without assuming guaranteed returns or uniform effects.

Jailbreak attempts and harmful prompts remain a challenge for the safe deployment of large language models. We study whether contrastively learned representations can support safety detection without training an additional downstream classifier. We propose Jailbreak Detection with Prototype Inference (JDPI), which uses binary safety labels to construct harmful and benign prototypes and makes predictions from relative prototype distances. JDPI uses only binary safety labels for encoder adaptation, prototype construction, and validation. In our setup, it uses fewer labeled examples than the classifier baseline (Method A) by avoiding the separate split used to train the downstream classifier. Across four benchmarks covering different input formats, contrastive fine-tuning improves JDPI's detection accuracy by 9.1-18.0 percentage points. Using the same encoder, JDPI achieves slightly higher ROC-AUC on one benchmark and stays within 0.017 of the baseline across all four. With dataset-specific adaptation, JDPI exceeds the released Llama Guard 3-8B baseline by 0.173-0.310 in ROC-AUC across the four benchmarks. In multi-turn replay on TomGibbs, JDPI uses accumulated user history as the conversation unfolds, achieving higher conversation-level accuracy than when it uses the current turn alone. Across 12 directed transfers, JDPI outperforms the classifier by an average of 1.59 percentage points in accuracy, demonstrating stronger cross-dataset robustness.

Agricultural activities depend on the timely coordi-nation of land, labour, machinery, information, and local services. In many rural settings, farmers identify workers and equipment through personal contacts and fragmented communication chan-nels. Such methods can make it difficult to discover available service providers beyond an immediate network, communicate work requirements consistently, and maintain a clear record of requests. Agricultural labourers and machinery owners can face a corresponding difficulty in communicating their availability to potential customers. This paper presents Kisan Sahayak, a theoretical, mobile-first agricultural marketplace designed to connect farmers, labourers, and machinery providers through a common web platform. The proposed system is organized around the MongoDB, Express.js, React.js, and Node.js (MERN) stack. Its conceptual capabilities include role-based profiles, location-aware discovery, farmer job postings, direct worker invitations, request acceptance or rejec-tion, wage negotiation, machinery listings, and service-request tracking. An optional artificial-intelligence assistance layer is proposed for multilingual platform guidance and explainable matching based on location, skills, availability, and stated pref-erences. The paper details the system architecture, data model, stake-holder workflows, marketplace rules, AI design, security and privacy controls, deployment considerations, and an evaluation framework. The contribution is an architectural and process model; no field trial, measured performance result, or im-plemented AI capability is claimed. The design is intended to provide a foundation for subsequent implementation and empirical evaluation in agricultural communities

When a capable model and a human reviewer cooperate on the same decision, which human still adds value? We argue this is a question about a single cognitive trait, metacognitive calibration: the alignment between a reviewer's behavioral confidence and the actual correctness of their judgments. We develop a trait theory of reviewer value to make it precise. The theory makes five claims: value is governed by calibration rather than by activity, speed, agreement, or tenure; calibration leaves observable traces in behavioral telemetry; those traces are non-diagnostic on their own, because the fast, low-revision signature of a calibrated expert is indistinguishable from that of a confident novice until it is gated by outcomes; human calibration and a model's self-knowledge are the same construct, so the joint system should defer to whichever agent is better calibrated on each item; and individual calibration is causally identifiable only above the level of the single judgment. We ground each claim in a six-month production window of an AI-assisted accounting system (541621 reviewer events, 483 reviewers), and find that a purely behavioral expertise profile inverts the ground truth, scoring an overconfident cohort (5.2 percent correction survival) higher than genuine experts (99.2 percent); that reviewer quality is flat across tenure, so the trait is not learned on the job; and that the same calibration logic that separates good from bad reviewers, applied to the model, concentrates 92.5 percent of human effort on genuine errors. We close with the boundary the theory must respect: under majority-vote aggregation, individual causal value is unidentifiable.

documents.abstract: The growing volume of topically similar papers makes it difficult to identify new work that can offer useful research insights or methodological guidance. We present KnowMe Paper Radar, a lightweight discovery tool that combines multiple sources of evidence into personalized reading priorities. Users specify topics, priorities, exclusions and dates; the system brings together topical relevance, recency, author research histories, collaboration paths and direction-specific institutional context. By exposing each score component and its supporting sources, KnowMe helps readers select promising papers for their current questions and discover relevant work beyond familiar authors. Automatic acquisition, version merging and graph-cache reuse keep this workflow convenient without large language model (LLM) inference during ordinary use. Experiments on 174,640 acquired records show more than threefold faster repeated context preparation, while cached abstracts improve normalized discounted cumulative gain at rank 10 (NDCG@10) from 0.412 to 0.598 on expert-judged retrieval tasks. Complementary analyses examine how the same accumulated records support semantic retrieval, research-history modeling and literature-grounded planning. A browser interface and a structured command-line interface (CLI) make these capabilities available to both researchers and research agents, positioning KnowMe as a practical upstream tool for literature-informed recursive self-improvement (RSI) workflows.

This chapter conceptualizes artificial intelligence (AI) in production engineering as a sociotechnical innovation. AI not only promises efficiency gains but also fundamentally reorganizes knowledge, work, and responsibility. Three case studies from assembly planning, laser beam welding, and predictive maintenance illustrate how algorithmic systems interact with embodied experiential knowledge and which value-laden decisions are embedded in objectives, thresholds, and routines. The analysis links technical core intuitions with perspectives on tacit knowledge, rationalization, and situated practice. A synthesis reveals three key tensions: the transformation of experience into formalized model knowledge, the shift of responsibility towards system design and operation, and the change in competency profiles towards data literacy and judgment competence. Regulatory requirements and organizational governance provide the guardrails for legitimacy and safety. From this, design principles are derived for trustworthy, auditable, and empowering AI that consistently combines transparency, human oversight, qualification, and organizational embedding.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: The advent of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education compels us to look beyond faculty members’ technological skills: it demands that we rethink the criteria that guide their professional judgment. With this in mind, this article builds a theoretical bridge between continuing education, pedagogical mediation, intellectual autonomy, and quality management, using Venezuelan universities as a case study. Through a critical review of academic literature, regulations, and international frameworks, the study identifies four interdependent pillars: professional identity linked to lifelong learning; pedagogical mediation under strict human supervision; ethical responsibility toward the sociocultural environment; and the institutional conditions necessary to sustain this innovation. Building on this, the study proposes integrating the dimensions of Being, Doing, Owing to Be, and Wanting to Be as a reflective compass for educators. In essence, it argues that educational quality does not improve through mere automation; rather, it requires pedagogical decisions to guide it, an awareness of its limits, and equitable access. Therefore, training teachers in AI requires a deeply humanistic and critical approach, supported by institutional policies that ensure responsible development and evaluation.

This research investigates whether a large language model or an autonomous AI Agent performs better at translating from English to Arabic, which is considered a low-resource language. The authors introduce WikiEn-Ar190, a new dataset of 190 carefully selected Wikipedia articles from 18 different areas, which were created and verified by two native Arabic speakers to ensure that they accurately reflect both meaning and style. Using this dataset, the study evaluates the translation quality of GPT-5-mini both as an independent neural translator and when used within a more complex process that includes self-assessment and improvement. As a standalone model, GPT-5-mini produced very fluent translations , achieving a COMET score of 0.8649 and receiving high human scores for adequacy, fluency, and style (averaging 4.53 out of 5). When used in a system that combined translation with self-assessment, it improved lexical accuracy by 28.76% (BLEU score of 22.83) while maintaining a similar level of semantic quality. These findings show that methods involving autonomous reasoning can improve translation consistency for language pairs with limited resources. Beyond the results, the approach offers a framework for evaluating and improving translations, potentially using them as assisting tools to expand the representation of low resource languages, such as Arabic, on the web.

Background The rapid integration of generative AI tools into higher education has raised concerns about problematic AI dependence and its links to academic procrastination, yet little is known about how these phenomena co-occur at the individual level among medical undergraduates. Objective This study identified latent profiles of AI dependence and academic procrastination among Chinese medical undergraduates, examined correlates of profile membership, and tested how profiles differ in positive acceptance and striving. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 530 undergraduates at two Chinese medical universities (March–May 2026). Latent profile analysis (LPA) was performed on seven dimension sum scores from the AIDep-22 and the Academic Procrastination Scale. Multinomial logistic regression examined demographic and AI-use correlates of profile membership, and the BCH approach compared positive acceptance and striving across profiles. Results A three-profile solution best fit the data: Class 1, “low dependence–low procrastination” (41.1%); Class 2, “high dependence–high procrastination” (25.8%); and Class 3, “functional/cognitive reliance–low procrastination” (33.0%). Relative to Class 1, membership in Class 3 was associated with first-choice major enrollment (OR for non-first-choice = 0.47, 95% CI 0.30–0.75), higher subjective AI familiarity (OR for low vs. high familiarity = 0.45, 95% CI 0.27–0.74) and more frequent AI use (OR for often vs. always = 0.42, 95% CI 0.26–0.68); only AI use frequency distinguished Class 2 from Class 1 (OR for often vs. always = 0.25, 95% CI 0.15–0.42). Class 2 scored significantly lower than Classes 1 and 3 on positive acceptance and striving (all p < 0.001). Conclusions AI dependence and procrastination do not covary uniformly: a substantial subgroup exhibits elevated functional and cognitive reliance on AI without severe procrastination, while a smaller subgroup shows co-occurring dependence and procrastination together with the lowest adaptive resources. Targeted support should prioritize the latter rather than treating all frequent AI users as uniformly at risk.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) across key societal sectors presents profound legal challenges, particularly regarding liability attribution and legal certainty. Operating autonomously with non-deterministic decision-making capabilities, AI deployment gives rise to risks such as copyright infringement, privacy breaches, and misinformation. Employing a normative juridical research method, this article examines whether AI can be held legally accountable under Indonesian law and evaluates the current statutory framework’s capacity to maintain legal certainty. The analysis demonstrates that Indonesian jurisprudence does not recognize AI as an independent legal subject, as it lacks moral agency and free choice. Consequently, legal responsibility remains anchored in traditional legal subjects—natural persons and corporate entities—operating in the capacity of Electronic Agents or Electronic System Providers (ESPs). Legal liability for AI-induced harm is channeled back to human developers and operating entities through established doctrines of vicarious and strict liability. Furthermore, while Indonesia currently lacks a standalone AI statute, legal certainty is preserved through an interlocking, multi-layered regulatory regime, including the Copyright Law, the Personal Data Protection Law, the Electronic Information and Transactions Law, the new Penal Code, the Government Regulation on Operation of Electronic Systems and Transactions, and the Circular Letter of the Minister of Communication and Information Technology on Artificial Intelligence Ethics. This study concludes that existing statutory frameworks provide enforceable sanctions, emphasizing that legal subjects must maintain strict compliance to mitigate technology-induced harm.

This conceptual paper introduces Layout-Dependent Geometry of Relational Maps, a structural constraint on what a viewer can infer from a diagram of connections. Two drawings can preserve the same station order and interchanges while giving the routes different lengths, placing stations at different distances, or making different groups stand out. A diagram may therefore give a passenger reliable grounds for choosing where to change trains while giving little indication of how far apart those stations lie above ground. The paper assesses a claim drawn from a map by asking whether the coding and layout preserve the particular relation the claim concerns. Redrawing a fixed set of connections can reveal which features change with placement. Even a cluster that persists across several drawings requires an independent check of what the positions encode. A claim about how viewers interpreted the cluster requires evidence about the viewers as well. The paper places this constraint alongside Jacques Bertin’s account of visual variables in graphics and examines two transit diagrams. Harry Beck’s 1933 London Underground diagram preserved station order and interchanges while redrawing distances. In a later study using London trip data from 1998 to 2005, Zhan Guo found that passengers were more likely to choose routes that appeared shorter on the map. The 1972 New York subway diagram, produced by Massimo Vignelli’s team at Unimark with Joan Charysyn as lead designer, drew Central Park as a square. The paper examines one rider’s complaint about wayfinding, John Tauranac’s criticism of the diagram’s geography, and its replacement in 1979. Part of the Equivalence and Interchangeability series within On Human Modeling, the paper has a prospective application in human–AI interaction. An AI assistant might draw a citation network from a set of papers. Readers can check a line between two papers against their references. If the assistant also claims that papers placed close together make similar arguments, that claim requires evidence from their texts or a placement rule that explicitly encodes such similarity.

Background High consequence infectious diseases (HCIDs) have high mortality rates and limited treatment options and require urgent co-ordinated public health response including sophisticated high-level isolation unit care. In the absence of a high-level isolation capacity in Ireland, the health systems of Ireland, Norway and Germany have agreed a collaborative HCID care arrangement where a patient diagnosed with a HCID in Ireland can be medically evacuated by Norwegian specialised air ambulance to Germany for ongoing care. These cross-border emergency arrangements and their coordination through EU mechanisms have not yet had to be exercised in real world circumstances. A full-scale real-time simulation exercise was devised to test pathways and use findings to improve the system. Methods This three-day, live, multi-service and cross-agency simulation tested multi-country interoperability, with over two hundred stakeholder participants. It was overseen by an international strategic exercise planning group and informed by the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC) simulation exercise cycle and national and ECDC guidance. Exercise evaluators assessed medical evacuation performance against predefined key performance indicators across the domains of international stakeholder activation, coordination and communication. Key Finding Such a large-scale exercise is resource-intensive, but feasible with cross-jurisdictional engagement. Intense cross-border planning was key to build relationships, clarify governance and develop harmonised guidance, pathways and procedures for testing in a safe environment. All eight high level objectives were achieved or partially achieved when measured against the pre-determined performance indicators. Findings including noting of discrepancies between different services in their high-level personal protective equipment (PPE) provision, and lack of 24-hour provision of services including laboratory diagnostics, specialised waste management, and occupational health. Lack of an agreed end-to-end transport protocol and waste-water management protocol required remedying. Following the exercise, strengthened governance and operational arrangements for preparedness and response include the development of a managed clinical network approach, enhanced operational capacity for key national services, and plans for a coordinated national HCID training and simulation programme. The findings have yielded key insights regarding interoperability across organisations and countries, and subsequent recommendations are likely to be transferable to other simulation programmes. To maintain optimal preparedness for high-stakes diseases and promote health security across Europe, partners should further incorporate international live simulation exercises to defend against cross-border health threats.

The integration of AI in Decision Support System faces a hard limit: automation bias (Cummings, 2004). While AI may outperforms human operators in certain tasks, the added value of keeping humans-in-the-loop becomes questionable if they merely validate AI decisions. However, the ideal tool should enable complementary team performance (CTP). CTP describes a situation where the human-AI (HAI) team overcomes both AI capacity and the operator alone in terms of performance, which is incompatible with automation bias. CTP describes a one-time performance, and is not easy to achieve: it means operators stay on their mind mostly when they are correct, and change their mind mostly when the AI is correct, which is optimistic, as shown in a recent meta-analysis (Vaccaro et al., 2024).However, one observation of CTP doesn’t preclude automation bias in the long-run. Beyond a static conception of performance, the dynamics of these interactions have been studied through several theoretical perspectives (Kumar et al., 2021; Williams et al., 2023; Gonzalez et al., 2026).The stress is often put on the evolution of trust in AI through time (Chong et al., 2022), but the issue of learning effects in the task, independent of trust, is poorly understood. What is the impact of AI assistance on human skill acquisition? This question has been mostly answered in educational contexts (Fan et al., 2025; Kosmyna et al., 2025), where the delegation of cognitive tasks to the AI would hinder the learning process of the children. In operational contexts, the fear of deskilling is often expressed by experts like physicists (Natali et al., 2025), but empirical evidence is missing, to our knowledge. This gap in the literature is understandable as the inquiry is challenging: in any domain, future experts are few, their tasks to learn are numerous, and the deployment of measurement settings on long duration might be difficult.To explore this question without conducting such longitudinal studies, we propose to build a model of human learning of a technical task with an advisor. Our work develop a simulation setting on a classification task to depict possible quantitative effects of advice-taking on performance evolution through time. This modeling scheme allowed us to investigate the impact of the advisor on skill development. While most people expect that a more accurate advisor would lead the learner to higher performances, Vaccaro et al. (2024) suggest that advisors with lesser performance would be more prone to inducing CTP. This claim follows from static experimental contexts: we hereby test it in a dynamical setting. We expect that in the long-run, deskilling could happen, and would affect not-only degraded-mode performance, but also maximal running performance. Is the performance of the advisor the main factor determining performance evolution, or could the assistants have an intrinsic complementarity with the learner, depending on their classification patterns? The type of AI could lead to different results, in terms of performance, reliance, and of dependence.
