documents.abstract: Background Maintaining safe workplace environments in manufacturing industries is important for ensuring employees' health and maintaining effective production performance. Research on environmental safety and occupational health and safety is extensive, but the association between environmental safety and production efficiency and whether employees' safety knowledge supports this relationship, has received limited attention. Methods Data were collected from two independent cross-sectional purposive samples of footwear production workers (Wave 1 and Wave 2; N = 385 each), 3 months apart, and analyzed separately using Hayes PROCESS macro model 7 to investigate the indirect association between environmental safety and production efficiency through occupational health and safety, and the moderating effect of safety knowledge, with a simple slope test used to probe the interaction. Total effects were estimated using model 4. Results Contrary to the hypothesized direction, the association between environmental safety and occupational health and safety was weaker at higher safety knowledge in both waves; the interaction was significant after correction for multiple testing in Wave 1 only. In Wave 1, the interaction was a crossover: environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety only at low safety knowledge, and the indirect effect on production efficiency was significant only at low safety knowledge. The direct and total effects were not significant. In Wave 2, environmental safety was positively related to occupational health and safety at all levels of safety knowledge, with the association weakening as knowledge increased. The indirect effect was significant at low, mean and high safety knowledge, and the direct and total effects were also significant, indicating partial mediation. Conclusion In both waves, environmental safety was indirectly associated with production efficiency through occupational health and safety, at least among workers with lower safety knowledge, and this indirect association was weaker among workers with higher safety knowledge. These cross-sectional findings suggest that safe working environments may be particularly relevant for workers with lower safety knowledge.

documents.abstract: Municipal solid waste workers operate in high-risk environments with limited institutional support, exposing them to diverse occupational hazards. This study explored occupational health and safety knowledge, practices, and experiences among municipal waste workers in Calabar, Nigeria, and examined the perceived impact of a health education intervention using a qualitative approach. A qualitative exploratory design was employed, involving Key Informant Interviews (KII) with 12 managers and Focus Group Discussions (FGDs) with 36 waste workers. Data were collected using semi-structured interview guides and analyzed using thematic analysis. Findings revealed low baseline knowledge of occupational hazards, poor safety practices, and systemic barriers such as inadequate provision of Personal Protective Equipment (PPE), weak monitoring, funding constraints, and poor prioritization of worker health. The intervention improved awareness and perceived understanding of occupational hazards and safety practices, although structural barriers persisted. The study concludes that health education enhances knowledge but must be complemented by systemic reforms, including provision of PPE, enforcement of safety policies, and improved worker welfare.

documents.abstract: Introduction Occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge is important for identifying worker training needs and informing workplace injury prevention strategies. However, immigrant workers are often treated as a homogeneous group despite differences in settlement duration, residency status, and previous training experiences that may influence their knowledge of workplace rights, responsibilities, and safe work practices. This exploratory study examined differences in OHS knowledge among immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years, immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years, and Canadian-born construction workers in Ontario, Canada. Methods A cross-sectional survey of 206 construction workers assessed OHS knowledge using scenario-based questions developed with reference to Ontario OHS requirements. Associations between OHS knowledge scores and participant characteristics were examined using univariable analyses and a generalized linear model. Results Immigrants residing in Ontario for >5 years had higher OHS knowledge scores than immigrants residing in Ontario for ≤5 years. Knowledge also differed by residency status, with Canadian citizens born outside Canada and permanent residents scoring higher than Canadian-born and temporary-resident participants. In the adjusted model, longer residence in Ontario, residency status, and previous OHS training outside Ontario were significantly associated with higher OHS knowledge scores. Discussion The findings demonstrate that OHS knowledge cannot be adequately characterized through a simple immigrant/non-immigrant distinction. Differences associated with settlement duration, residency status, and previous training highlight important heterogeneity among construction workers and may help identify OHS educational and prevention needs. Future research should evaluate whether targeted interventions addressing these differences improve safety practices and occupational health outcomes.

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Large Language Model (LLM) inference systems has led to significant improvements in serving efficiency. However, our systematic analysis reveals that current evaluation methodologies suffer from fundamental flaws that mask critical performance issues and impede scientific progress. Through a comprehensive examination of recent systems, we identify recurring pitfalls in evaluation practices across three key dimensions: Baseline Fairness, Evaluation Setup, and Metric Design. These pitfalls are uniquely problematic for LLM inference due to its dual-phase nature combining prefill and decode operations, heterogeneous workloads, and strict temporal requirements. We demonstrate how implementation differences frequently obscure algorithmic contributions, how workload selection often fails to represent production scenarios, and how metric normalization can hide substantial performance variability that directly impacts user experience. Traditional metrics derived from the classical machine learning serving setup fail to capture the autoregressive generation characteristics essential to LLM inference, leading to misleading conclusions about system performance. To address these challenges, we provide a comprehensive checklist of best practices and methodological recommendations for robust LLM inference evaluations. To demonstrate the practical application of our methodology, we present a case study of speculative decoding evaluation - a technique whose non-uniform token generation patterns with bursts during accepted predictions and delays during verification failures fundamentally confound conventional metrics. Our work establishes a rigorous foundation for evaluation methodology that can accelerate progress in LLM inference systems by ensuring meaningful comparisons, reproducible results, and metrics that reflect real-world requirements.

Large language models are increasingly used to create stories for children. Since bedtime stories can shape children's perceptions of social roles, this raises concerns about whether LLMs adapt narrative portrayals according to the intended recipient's gender. We conducted a large-scale study to examine gender stereotyping in LLM-generated bedtime stories. Using matched daughter/son prompts and a five-generation design, we analyze 62,873 retained stories from 16 LLMs across 35 country settings and 12 narrator roles. We introduce a multi-level evaluation framework combining context-adjusted lexical rate contrasts, relative stereotype alignment, narrator-recipient interaction analysis, human evaluation, and representation-level interventions to examine both the consistency and interpretability of these differences. Our results reveal systematic differences in narrative framing: son-directed stories emphasize higher agency and lower communion compared to daughter-directed stories. While narrator gender expresses limited moderation on these patterns, high sociability exhibits a more pronounced interaction. Human evaluations demonstrate consistent agreement, although correspondence with lexical measures varies across narrative dimensions. Additionally, hidden-state analyses reveal decodable recipient-gender information. These findings demonstrate persistent yet context-dependent representational disparities in LLM-generated children's stories and motivate narrative-specific bias evaluation beyond short-form benchmarks.

documents.abstract: Current diabetic retinopathy management relies primarily on contemporaneous severity grading and does not directly quantify the short-term risk of vision-threatening complications. We developed and internally evaluated image-based artificial intelligence models for one-year prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity, proliferative diabetic retinopathy (PDR) and center-involved diabetic macular edema (ci-DME) using retinal imaging acquired during routine care.The prospective multicenter EviRed cohort included 3,183 patients with diabetes, 8,520 visits and 16,509 eye-level observations collected across 14 French hospitals. Device-specific ensembles were developed for ultra-widefield color fundus photography (CLARUS500 and OPTOS) and OCT angiography (CIRRUS5000 and PLEX Elite9000). Predictions from individual images and both eyes were aggregated at the patient-visit level. Participants were partitioned at the patient level into adevelopment set (65\%) and a held-out test set (35\%).For prediction of diabetic retinopathy severity at the subsequent annual visit, OPTOS and CLARUS500 achieved quadratic weighted kappa values of 0.866 (95\% confidence interval, 0.842--0.878) and 0.852 (0.830--0.877), respectively. For incident ci-DME, CIRRUS5000 achieved the highest discrimination (AUC, 0.826; 0.770--0.878), whereas PLEX Elite9000 yielded the highest AUC point estimate for incident PDR (0.877; 0.807--0.950). Late fusion did not consistently outperform the strongest device-specific model. In secondary complete-case analyses, observed ci-DME incidence increased across quartiles of the image-derived risk score, reaching 19.7--30.4\% in the highest-risk quartile. AI models also achieved higher AUC point estimates than unassisted expert risk assessments for both complications, although these comparisons were exploratory.Retinal imaging acquired at a single routine-care visit therefore contains information associated with diabetic retinopathy severity and vision-threatening complications one year later. These findings support image-based short-term risk stratification, while external validation, calibration and prospective clinical utility assessment remain necessary before deployment.

Background. Ambient clinical AI — software that listens to a consultation and drafts the clinical note, often called an AI scribe — is now a flagship use of artificial intelligence in healthcare. Most tools delivering it are proprietary and cloud-based: consultation audio leaves the building, errors cannot be independently characterised, and the clinician who signs the note answers for output nobody outside the vendor can examine. Open, fully local alternatives that a clinician or researcher can inspect, run and modify remain rare. Objective. This paper reports OpenConsult, an open-source AI scribe with live clinical decision support that runs entirely on one machine in the consulting room and is inspectable end to end, and describes its formative evaluation. Methods. Evaluation was formative and used synthetic consultations only (scripted and acted). Automated tests ran fifteen scripted consultations with pre-written marking schemes, checking transcription quality gates, the urgency alarm’s behaviour across emergency and routine scripts, and whether every cited claim in a note points to a real transcript line. Five acted consultations followed in a real consulting room, and the AI assistants that built the system ran an adversarial security audit under the developer’s direction. The work is reported against the applicable DECIDE-AI items, one stage before live clinical evaluation. Results. OpenConsult is a fully local, open-source consultation assistant, built by a practising general practitioner directing AI coding assistants, running on a single consumer graphics card. It transcribes the consultation live and separates the speakers, drafts a structured clinical note with every sentence linked to its supporting transcript words, runs live decision support whose urgency alarm is shown only to the doctor, drafts referral letters, and offers a supervised spoken history-taking mode. In generated notes, 301 of 302 citations pointed to real transcript lines — an existence check, with clinical faithfulness unmeasured pending independent rating; the one uncited claim was flagged for manual checking. The urgency alarm fired in all eight scripted emergencies and stayed silent in six of seven routine consultations. Five acted consultations surfaced five defects the automated checks had missed, four of them serious; all were fixed, each pinned by a regression test. The security audit returned twelve findings, including one critical vulnerability, fixed and verified before any public exposure. Conclusions. OpenConsult is a working, auditable proof of concept — not yet a validated clinical tool — released for research and education only, with real patient care out of scope. It is intended as an open research instrument: it records whether the reviewing clinician opened the cited evidence before approving, how long review takes, and every revision of its decision support, making human review of ambient clinical AI measurable. Independent, prospective evaluation is required before any step toward care.

documents.abstract: Building autonomous agents that continually explore open worlds and acquire new capabilities through experience is a long-standing aspiration in artificial intelligence. Existing research often pursues lifelong learning within predefined tasks, curricula, or objectives, with self-improvement largely confined to individual agents. We introduce OpenKAGE, an agent-group evolution framework for open-ended lifelong learning. Within this framework, agents autonomously explore open worlds and continually acquire new capabilities by accumulating and reusing knowledge from their own interactions and the experience of others. OpenKAGE builds on two key mechanisms: (1) a two-layer knowledge representation, with a memory layer for situated memories and an experience layer for transferable experience and skills that retains the applicability conditions needed for reuse; and (2) a knowledge-sharing mechanism that semantically consolidates textual experience into a continuously evolving shared knowledge graph, while executable skills are shared verbatim. In Minecraft, OpenKAGE supports open-ended lifelong learning, enabling agent groups to sustain exploration and reach advanced technological milestones. Furthermore, the accumulated knowledge can be transferred to a newly initialized agent group on a different backbone model, improving its survival and exploration progress.

Artificial intelligence is entering the everyday work of secondary schools. Teachers encounter AI-based tools both in classroom organisation and in feedback or adaptation tasks. As these tools become more visible in school practice, their educational role and practical value need to be examined in relation to the conditions of real classrooms. This is especially relevant in classes with varied learning characteristics, where students differ in pace and readiness to participate. In these settings, AI may help teachers adapt instructional material and provide more individualised support. Its value, however, depends on professional judgement and on how each tool is connected to pedagogical purpose. This paper examines opportunities and challenges related to the use of artificial intelligence in secondary education. The planned study will use teachers’ accounts to examine how AI tools are understood and used in secondary school practice. It is designed as a qualitative inquiry based on semi-structured interviews with secondary education teachers, with the interview material examined thematically. Through teachers’ accounts, the study will explore how AI is understood in relation to lesson preparation and student support, while also examining what makes its use difficult in day-to-day teaching. The paper approaches AI as a tool whose usefulness depends on classroom context and teachers’ pedagogical decisions.

documents.abstract: Virtual reality (VR) and augmented reality (AR) are moving from experimental demonstrations to operational tools in military aviation. This article examines the main opportunities these technologies offer in six areas: immersive flight and mission training, cockpit and helmet-mounted displays, live-virtual-constructive training, aircraft maintenance, mission planning and debriefing, and human-performance training. Using an analytical review of academic and professional literature, the study compares the potential benefits of each application area with its principal technical and human-factors limitations. The findings show that VR offers the clearest near-term value in cost-effective procedural and tactical training, while AR offers the greatest long-term value in airborne information display and in maintenance support. Simulator sickness, latency, registration accuracy, cybersecurity and the need for validated transfer-of-training evidence remain the key barriers. The article concludes with practical recommendations for armed forces and military education institutions that wish to adopt these technologies in a phased and evidence-based way.

Urban biodiversity loss is increasingly framed as a governance challenge with intertwined ecological and social dimensions, yet little is known about who participates in local biodiversity planning, what authority that participation carries, and whether plans recognize and address disproportionate harms. This study presents the first comparative analysis at this scale of participation in Local Biodiversity Strategies and Action Plans (LBSAPs), examining 98 plans from 98 municipalities across 26 countries. Using a hybrid methodology combining large language model-assisted verbatim extraction with manual coding (96.4% extraction accuracy), plans were assessed across four dimensions: participant recognition, participatory mechanisms, authorship, and transparency. Of the 98 plans, 71 (72%) documented some participatory mechanism, but only 18 (18%) granted participants any authority over plan content, and only 2 (2%) shared control over resources. Authorship was concentrated in city governments (93 of 98 plans), and 39 cities (40%) provided no transparency about participatory processes. Knowledge-holder positioning was dominated by scientists (M = 0.60 on a 0–1 scale) while Indigenous peoples (M = 0.08), marginalized groups (M = 0.01), and youth (M = 0.03) were systematically excluded. A distributive analysis revealed a marginalized-specific redress gap: 16 plans recognized marginalized groups as bearing environmental harm, but only 4 of those plans offered programmatic response; a 75% recognition-without-remedy rate not seen for any other actor type. These findings indicate that prevailing LBSAP governance architectures may constrain conservation effectiveness, by excluding the situated knowledge of communities most affected by biodiversity loss, and may reproduce environmental injustice, by acknowledging disproportionate harms without acting on them. Governance reforms that meaningfully redistribute participatory authority are needed to advance both biodiversity outcomes and equitable urban conservation.

Plant genomics with a hybrid classical-quantum model Artificial intelligence and quantum computing for the digital design of plant genomes Italian patent application no. 102026000034324, filed on 18 November 2026. Inventor, applicant and sole rights holder: Paolo Ciccolella. This invention proposes combining artificial intelligence and quantum computing to explore possible combinations of plant DNA and identify those worth investigating further. For businesses interested in plant genomics, the idea is to provide early guidance for computational design: turning a vast number of possibilities into selected, evaluated and documented digital candidates. The challenge is easy to picture. If DNA is a large instruction book, studying alternative versions of some passages means comparing many combinations. Three alternatives for each of twenty regions already produce more than three billion possibilities. The method tackles this complexity by dividing the work between a classical computer, two AI models and a quantum search component. HOW THE HYBRID MODEL WORKS The idea is to choose one alternative for each DNA region being studied, put the choices together and evaluate the resulting combination. Everything happens on a computer. The process follows six steps. • Prepare the data. The computer starts with a digital version of the plant’s DNA, called a reference genome. It identifies the regions to study and organises the available alternative sequences for each one, recording where they come from. • Give each alternative an initial score. The first AI model examines each alternative separately. Having learned from other cases, it can provide guidance before any complete combination in the new case has been evaluated. The computer also measures similarity between the ends of sequences that will be placed next to one another. These scores and measurements define the selection problem. [B12] • Search for combinations. The quantum component receives this problem expressed in numbers. It uses QAOA, an algorithm whose role is to propose combinations while seeking to favour those with better scores. Qubits represent the possible choices; the DNA sequences remain on the classical computer, which sets and updates the algorithm’s parameters. [B11] • Evaluate the whole combination. The computer checks that each combination selects exactly one alternative per region and assembles valid choices into a digital candidate. The second AI model evaluates the complete candidate, including relationships between its parts that the first AI model could not observe when examining them separately. • Guide the next search. The system compares the overall evaluation with the score predicted at the start and uses the difference to update the search. When only a few results are available, it limits the correction’s influence to avoid relying too heavily on sparse information. • Return verifiable proposals. For each selected candidate, the system retains the chosen sequences, their provenance and the evaluations performed. It also records a digital fingerprint, a code used to check the content. Researchers can reconstruct the proposal and understand how it was selected. If necessary data are missing, the system flags this. A concrete example: the patent uses the digital reference for Micro-Tom tomato and considers three regions, each with three alternatives created for the test. There are 3 × 3 × 3 = 27 possible combinations. The search uses a nine-qubit quantum circuit simulated on a classical computer. This tests the computational method without producing plants. [B14] INDUSTRIAL APPLICATIONS The patent describes the production of verifiable digital representations of candidate genomes. Its industrial role lies in designing and selecting hypotheses, ahead of experimental work. Applications across sectors require data and models suited to the objectives under study. • NGT and assisted evolution techniques. NGTs, or new genomic techniques, include approaches known in Italy as TEA, meaning assisted evolution techniques, which enable targeted changes to genetic material. The proposed method could support research by comparing genomic hypotheses before experimental work. For seed and biotechnology companies, the prospect is to build a reasoned set of digital candidates for further investigation within NGT/TEA programmes. • Seed industry and variety development. For seed companies and research teams, the method could support the preliminary selection of combinations for further study. Research objectives could include drought or salinity tolerance, disease resistance and yield stability. Its contribution would be to establish research priorities while preserving the reasoning behind them. • Fresh produce and food processing. Computational design could focus on commercial characteristics such as product quality, shelf life and processing suitability. Tomato, pepper and aubergine are examples of supply chains that future projects could address, connecting growers’ and processors’ needs with the criteria used to evaluate candidates. • Nutraceuticals and plant ingredients. One possible development concerns plants of interest for functional ingredients, extracts and bioactive compounds. The method could explore genomic combinations in programmes focused, for example, on pigments or plant metabolites, providing documented candidates to guide subsequent analysis. • Plant biotechnology and industrial raw materials. For crops intended for oils, fibres or biomass, the method could help compare genomic hypotheses against supply chain objectives. Reconstructible digital records would support information exchange between teams developing the models and those planning subsequent experimental work. • Bioinformatics and computing centres. The most direct application is within the information systems of laboratories, computing centres and plant genomics businesses. The process could underpin software modules or analytical services that explore combinations and return candidates with scores and execution logs, integrating quantum search into the workflow. Introduction As part of a strategy to increase magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) capacity, the UK government funded the purchase of manufacturer artificial intelligence (AI) MRI image reconstruction software on MRI scanners. It aimed to reduce scan duration without compromising image quality and has been widely installed on clinical MRI scanners across the UK. Methods This is a mixed methods study, using an initial questionnaire to quantify opinions followed by focus groups of responders to further explore their views on technical issues. Patient views on the use of AI in MRI image reconstruction for reducing acquisition times, and more generally in their MRI pathway, were assessed. Results Study participants prefer improved image quality over faster acquisition times. If reducing acquisition times with AI, they feel it should only be used if extremely accurate images can be ascertained. They are uncomfortable with the use of manufacturer AI software for image reconstruction where accuracy is not stated and would like to be told about the use of AI in MRI. Conclusions Many participants felt that manufacturer AI software for MRI image reconstruction may be used only if a high accuracy is demonstrated, and if the training data is representative of the patient population, to not exacerbate health inequalities. This information is not currently given by manufacturers, which made the patient representatives concerned. Implication for practice •Local validation of AI image reconstruction software may make patients more confident about its use. •AI patient information materials should be accessible and discuss accuracy, and radiographers can be trained to help inform and reassure patients. •Engagement with all clinical stakeholders in MRI should be undertaken to understand their views on AI, and how manufacturer AI software should be implemented.

documents.abstract: Over the past decade, the innovative convergence of cloud computing, natural language processing (NLP), and large language models (LLM) has triggered a paradigm shift in human-computer interaction. This study aims to conceptually review and propose a research design to objectively analyze the effect of security and privacy perceptions on the use of AI as a venting medium. The proposed method is a conceptual quantitative research design with a correlational approach, planned for Generation Z respondents. Based on a literature synthesis of referenced studies, the findings indicate a highly significant positive correlation between dispositional shame and self-disclosure to artificial intelligence (r = 0.337, p < 0.001, n = 182). The conceptual review concludes that AI operates effectively as a complementary screening instrument but risks triggering an atrophy of social resilience, thus necessitating juridical protection through the Personal Data Protection Law (UU PDP).

documents.abstract: Digital inclusion with generative AI depends not only on educators’ access to tools but on how they use them. Comparing the benefits educators perceive with the uses they report may reveal gaps between what educators believe AI can do and how they use it in teaching. In this exploratory secondary analysis of survey data from 293 Minnesota PK-12 and higher education educators, we compared endorsement of improved accessibility for diverse learners as a benefit of generative AI with reported use of AI to enhance accessibility for students with disabilities. Because the items differ in scope and target population, the comparison describes response proportions, not a failure to act on a belief. Among 160 AI-using educators who answered both items, 133 (83.1%) endorsed the benefit and 51 (31.9%) reported the use (McNemar exact p < 0.001). Subgroup differences were not detected, though power was limited. Among all AI users, self-rated competence was associated with reported accessibility use (44.0% vs. 27.9%; adjusted OR = 2.31, 95% CI [1.13, 4.73]); among endorsers, the estimate was imprecise. Keyword-selected open-ended responses more often described general differentiation and language support than disability-specific use. We discuss measurement implications and propose supports as hypotheses for evaluation.

Background Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used in medical training, but evidence from African residency programs is scarce. We assessed how internal medicine residents in Ethiopia use GenAI and how they perceive its impact on clinical learning and clinical decision-making. Methods We conducted an explanatory sequential mixed-methods study consisting of a national cross-sectional online survey of internal medicine residents (June to August 2026), followed by two focus group discussions (FGDs) with 10 residents at two universities (September 2026) to explain the survey findings. Perceived impact was measured with five-point Likert items and two composite scores (learning, five items; decision-making, eight items). Associations with frequency of use were tested with chi-square or Fisher's exact tests. FGD data were organized deductively into categories based on the survey topics. Results Of 252 respondents from 18 institutions, 98.8% had used GenAI and 75.4% used it daily; ChatGPT was used by 91.6% of users. The mean composite score for perceived impact on clinical learning was 3.83 out of 5 (70.7% high) and for clinical decision-making 3.86 out of 5 (67.7% high). Agreement was highest for improved differential diagnosis (90.8%), learning efficiency (81.9%) and support for self-directed learning (79.5%), and lowest for ward-round performance (64.3%) and confidence in complex cases (71.4%). Daily use was more frequent among residents with more than three hours of daily internet use (82.3% versus 66.7% to 67.4%; p = 0.024) and was not associated with age, sex, marital status, year of residency, device access or formal training. In the FGDs, residents described GenAI as a fast, supportive tool for learning and clinical work, as an aid to reasoning and not a replacement for physician judgment, and as a possible threat to independent learning. Conclusions Residents perceive GenAI as helpful for self-directed learning and diagnostic reasoning while keeping final responsibility for clinical decisions. These findings reflect perceptions and not measured outcomes, so objective evaluation of its effects on learning and clinical performance is needed.
